subject: Polity
description: Covers Electoral College, Pardoning power, Veto types.

questions.stem: According to Article 54 of the Indian Constitution, the President of India is elected by an Electoral College consisting of:

options.option_text: Only the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including Delhi and Puducherry)
All members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament and all State Legislative Assemblies
Only the elected members of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
The citizens of India directly through a general election

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The President is indirectly elected. The Electoral College strictly excludes NOMINATED members (like the 12 nominated members of Rajya Sabha or Anglo-Indians previously in Assemblies). It also strictly excludes members of State Legislative COUNCILS (Vidhan Parishads) because not all states have them, which would skew the vote. It only includes ELECTED members of the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies (including the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry, added by the 70th Amendment).
DECOY BUSTING: Nominated members do not participate in the ELECTION of the President. (However, ironically, nominated members of Parliament DO participate in the IMPEACHMENT of the President). 
EXAM INSIGHT: The value of an MLA's vote is not 1; it is calculated based on the population of their state (using the 1971 census). This ensures a state like UP has more weight than a small state like Sikkim, reflecting actual population size.

questions.stem: Under Article 72 of the Constitution, the President of India has the power to grant pardons. Which of the following statements regarding this pardoning power is CORRECT?

options.option_text: The President can pardon death sentences and sentences issued by Court-Martials (military courts)
The President's pardoning power is absolutely independent and does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers
The President can only pardon offenses against State laws, not Union laws
The Governor of a State shares the exact same pardoning powers as the President, including pardoning death sentences

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 72 grants the President broad clemency powers. Unlike a State Governor (Article 161), the President has two exclusive pardoning powers: 1) He can pardon a death sentence (a Governor can only suspend or commute it, not completely pardon it). 2) He can pardon sentences handed down by Court-Martials (military courts), which Governors have no jurisdiction over.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- The President cannot act independently; he must exercise this power on the advice of the Union Cabinet.
- The President pardons offenses against UNION laws, not State laws (unless it's a death penalty case).
EXAM INSIGHT: There are five types of clemency: Pardon (completely clears the convict), Commutation (substituting a harsh punishment with a lighter one), Remission (reducing the period of sentence without changing its character), Respite (lesser sentence due to special facts like pregnancy), and Reprieve (temporary stay on execution).

questions.stem: Which type of Veto power does the President of India NOT possess?

options.option_text: Qualified Veto
Absolute Veto
Suspensive Veto
Pocket Veto

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: A 'Qualified Veto' is one that can be overridden by the legislature only with a HIGHER majority than was used to pass the bill originally. The US President has a Qualified Veto. The Indian President DOES NOT have this. 
DECOY BUSTING: The Indian President has three vetos:
1) Absolute Veto: Withholding assent entirely (usually used for Private Member bills or if the cabinet resigns).
2) Suspensive Veto: Returning the bill for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again with an ORDINARY majority, the President must sign it.
3) Pocket Veto: Keeping the bill pending indefinitely without taking any action (famously used by President Zail Singh in 1986 on the Post Office Bill).
EXAM INSIGHT: The President has NO veto power whatsoever in respect of a Constitutional Amendment Bill. The 24th Amendment Act (1971) made it obligatory for the President to give his assent to them.

questions.stem: Under Article 55(2)(b) of the Constitution, the value of each vote of an elected Member of a State Legislative Assembly in the Presidential election is calculated by dividing the State's population by which of the following?

options.option_text: The number of elected MLAs in that State's Assembly, multiplied by 1000
The number of Rajya Sabha seats allocated to that State, multiplied by 1000
The total elected members of Parliament from that State, multiplied by 1000
The total seats in both Houses of that State's Legislature, multiplied by 1000

questions.explanation: Article 55(2)(b) specifies: value of each MLA's vote = (population of State) ÷ (elected MLAs × 1000), rounded to the nearest whole number. Option C is the most tempting error — candidates confuse MLAs with elected MPs. Nominated members of the Assembly are excluded, and Rajya Sabha seat allocation (Option B) has no role in this formula.

questions.stem: The President of India is constitutionally required to address both Houses of Parliament assembled together at the commencement of specific sessions each year. Which Article of the Constitution mandates this special address?

options.option_text: Article 85 — governing sessions, prorogation and dissolution of Parliament
Article 86 — granting the President the right to address either or both Houses
Article 87 — mandating the President's special address at the commencement of sessions
Article 88 — governing the rights of Ministers and Attorney-General in Parliament

questions.explanation: Article 87(1) imposes an obligation — the President 'shall address' both Houses together at commencement of the first session after each Lok Sabha general election and at the first session of each year. Article 86 (the most tempting distractor) only confers a general permissive right to address Parliament but creates no mandatory duty. The two articles are often confused in exams.

questions.stem: A Bill is certified as a Money Bill by the Speaker of Lok Sabha and presented to the President for assent under Article 111. Which of the following courses of action is constitutionally unavailable to the President?

options.option_text: Granting assent to the Bill as certified by the Speaker of Lok Sabha
Returning the Bill to Parliament with a message requesting reconsideration
Withholding assent from the Bill without returning it to Parliament
Delaying action on the Bill for an indefinite period before signifying assent

questions.explanation: The proviso to Article 111 explicitly restricts the return option to Bills that are 'not a Money Bill' — the President may return only non-Money Bills. Returning a Money Bill is thus expressly forbidden. Option C (withholding assent) is technically undesirable but not expressly prohibited in the same way. Option D exploits the absence of a time limit in Article 111, which creates the informal 'pocket veto' space.

questions.stem: The President of India made a Reference to the Supreme Court under Article 143(1) on a question of constitutional importance. Which statement correctly describes the legal effect of the Court's response?

options.option_text: The Supreme Court must answer and its opinion is binding on the President and all courts
The Supreme Court may decline to answer, and any opinion tendered is advisory not binding
The opinion carries the same binding force as a Supreme Court decree under Article 141
The President must act on the opinion within 90 days or the reference lapses automatically

questions.explanation: Article 143(1) uses the word 'may' for both the reference and the Court's response — the Supreme Court may report its opinion; it is not bound to answer. The advisory opinion has no binding force, unlike judgments under Article 136. This was affirmed in the Special Courts Bill Reference (1978). Option A conflates advisory jurisdiction with the binding precedent rule under Article 141, which applies only to regular judicial decisions.

questions.stem: Article 78(c) of the Constitution confers a specific but often-overlooked power upon the President relative to the Council of Ministers. Which of the following correctly describes this power?

options.option_text: The President may summon the Cabinet for an emergency sitting to ratify any Ordinance
The President may require the PM to send to Cabinet any matter a Minister decided alone
The President may override a Cabinet decision that conflicts with a Presidential directive
The President may directly call for files from any Ministry, bypassing the PM

questions.explanation: Article 78(c) states the President can require the Prime Minister to submit for Cabinet consideration any matter on which a decision was taken by a single Minister but was not considered by the Cabinet collectively. This is a check against individual ministerial overreach. Options A, C, and D have no constitutional basis — the President has no power to summon Cabinet, override Cabinet decisions, or bypass the PM to requisition departmental files.

questions.stem: To prefer a charge of impeachment against the President under Article 61(2), a resolution must be moved in either House of Parliament. What is the correct combination of procedural thresholds required?

options.option_text: Notice signed by one-third of members, passed by two-thirds of total membership
Notice signed by one-fourth of members, passed by two-thirds of total membership
Notice signed by one-half of members, passed by two-thirds of members present and voting
Notice signed by one-fourth of members, passed by simple majority of total membership

questions.explanation: Article 61(2)(a) requires at least 14 days' written notice signed by not less than one-fourth of the total membership. Article 61(2)(b) then requires the resolution to be passed by not less than two-thirds of the total membership — not merely two-thirds of those present and voting. Option A (one-third notice) confuses the notice threshold with that for special resolutions elsewhere. Option D uses 'simple majority' which is wholly insufficient for a presidential impeachment charge.

questions.stem: The concept of 'pocket veto' as practised by the President of India — most notably by President Zail Singh against the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 — arises from which specific constitutional lacuna?

options.option_text: Article 111 sets no deadline for the President to act on a Bill presented for assent
Article 123 lets the President keep a parallel Ordinance alive to negate the Bill
Article 143 lets the President refer any Bill to the Supreme Court, stalling assent
Article 85(2) lets the President prorogue Parliament indefinitely, keeping Bills alive

questions.explanation: Unlike the US Constitution, which gives the President a mandatory 10-day window, Article 111 of the Indian Constitution prescribes no time limit for the President to signify assent, withhold assent, or return a Bill. This silence creates the pocket veto — the Bill is held indefinitely without any formal action. Options B, C, and D each describe genuine constitutional powers but none creates the open-ended assent gap that enables the pocket veto technique.
